title: Self-powered bioelectronics for peripheral nerve regeneration: Electroactive materials, energy transduction, and therapeutic mechanisms

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Self-powered bioelectronics for peripheral nerve regeneration: Electroactive materials, energy transduction, and therapeutic mechanisms》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · p0045】The novelty of this review lies in providing a comprehensive translational framework for self-powered bioelectronics in peripheral nerve regeneration. Beyond summarizing recent advances, a critical and focused comparison of self-electrified galvanic, triboelectric, and piezoelectric platforms specifically for peripheral nerve repair remains limited. It critically examines these three approaches through a common material: interface, device, and biology framework, covering their energy-transduction mechanisms, material and device design, electrical stimulation characteristics, and preclinical evidence for nerve regeneration. Particular emphasis is placed on how the energy source and device architecture determine the nature, duration, and controllability of the electrical stimulus delivered, and how these factors relate to biological responses and functional outcomes. Rather than comparing platforms primarily by unloaded voltage or other isolated device-level metrics, we consider stimulation dose, experimental conditions, regenerative endpoints, degradation behavior, safety, and translational requirements. Through this framework, the review aims to distinguish demonstrated regenerative effects from device-level performance claims and identify the key considerations for developing clinically relevant self-powered electroactive platforms for peripheral nerve repair. The clinical value of these platforms depends on establishing the delivered stimulation dose, long-term safety, and the reproducibility of functional benefit. Its specific contribution is to connect energy dependence and device design to the strength of clinical regenerative evidence and the requirements for translation, rather than ranking technologies by unloaded voltage.

【Introduction · p0015】The peripheral nervous system (PNS) serves as an indispensable communication network, transmitting motor commands, relaying sensory information, and regulating autonomic functions between the central nervous system and effector organs [1]. Despite its functional sophistication, peripheral nerve tissue is profoundly vulnerable to traumatic, compressive, and ischemic insults. Peripheral nerve injuries (PNIs) represent one of the most debilitating categories of neurological trauma, with an estimated annual incidence of 13–23 per 100,000 individuals, often resulting in devastating sensory deficits, motor paralysis, and chronic neuropathic pain [[1], [2], [3], [4], [5]]. Trauma and other insults can disrupt peripheral nerve structure and function [6]. Following transection or severe crush injury, the distal axonal segment undergoes Wallerian degeneration, an orchestrated cascade in which the cytoskeleton disassembles and Schwann cells (SCs) transition into an activated repair phenotype. These repair SCs proliferate and align within residual basal lamina tubes to form “Bands of Büngner" that guide regenerating sprouts, while recruited macrophages help clear axonal and myelin debris [7,8]. However, axonal regrowth proceeds at approximately 1–3 mm per day; protracted regeneration often leads to SC phenotype loss, tube collapse, and irreversible muscle atrophy. Recovery remains variable even after surgical repair [3]. The consequences of severe peripheral nerve injury result in formidable challenges due to chronic pain, such as neuroma formation [9]. Early diagnosis is crucial to monitor healing stages after severe neuropathic injury, which provides key physiological and pathological insights for timely medical interventions. To address these challenges, multifunctional peripheral nerve interfaces that employ bioreabsorbable electronic platform materials facilitate nerve regeneration and pain management. This biodegradable nerve interface relies on its flexibility integrated with wireless technology for signal amplification, digitization, and remote transmission, potentially reducing the need for removal surgery when whole-device bioresorption is established.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Self-powered bioelectronics for peripheral nerve regeneration: Electroactive materials, energy transduction, and therapeutic mechanisms》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Materials selection for self-electrified galvanic devices · p0065】Material selection plays a central role in optimizing galvanic bioelectronic devices, particularly in the design of anodes, cathodes, electrolytes, and packaging materials. In biodegradable galvanic systems, metals with sufficiently separated electrochemical potentials are selected to establish a stable redox couple while maintaining biocompatibility and predictable bioresorption profiles [53]. For instance, Mg is frequently employed as the sacrificial anode because of its highly negative electrochemical potential, favorable biodegradability, and demonstrated compatibility with neural tissues, whereas FeMn alloys or Mo can function as cathodic materials due to their slower corrosion rates and stable electrochemical behavior in physiological electrolytes [54,55]. Appropriate electrode pairing, therefore, requires a comprehensive understanding of the electrochemical characteristics of candidate materials to ensure optimal device performance. Integration of theoretical modeling with advanced material-processing techniques further enables the development of electrodes with high electrical conductivity, robust mechanical integrity, and excellent electrochemical performance [56]. Although bioresorbable metals such as Mg, Zn, and Fe readily degrade in vivo, their corrosion byproducts, particularly elevated local hydroxide ion (OH−) concentrations, may induce tissue alkalization and adversely affect cellular activity [53]. Consequently, both the electrode materials and their degradation products or electrochemical byproducts must be carefully considered. In addition, chronic inflammatory responses and fibrotic capsule formation remain persistent challenges following implantation, highlighting the importance of rigorous evaluation of material biocompatibility to minimize long-term inflammatory reactions.

【Materials for triboelectric layers · p0085】TENG design for nerve repair requires the selection of triboelectric material pairs capable of maximizing charge transfer efficiency while maintaining biodegradability and biocompatibility [61,63]. Materials used for triboelectric layer fabrication can generally be classified as organic or inorganic. For example, polymers such as PLGA, (polycaprolactone (PCL), silk fibroin, and cellulose derivatives can be paired to achieve useful charge transfer; the relative triboelectric polarity depends on the counter-material and surface conditions. Materials used for triboelectric layer fabrication can generally be classified as organic or inorganic [61,63,64]. Among organic materials, polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) is widely employed as a TENG substrate due to its biocompatibility, mechanical flexibility, and ease of fabrication, making it well-suited for implantable bioelectronic applications [[64], [65], [66]]. Fluorinated polymers such as polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) and fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP), commonly referred to as Teflon, exhibit strong negative triboelectric polarity and are therefore highly effective for charge generation when paired with appropriate tribo-positive materials. For biodegradable implantable systems, polymers including PLGA, PCL, PLA, PGA, and silk fibroin are frequently explored as tribopositive layers, while electronegative cellulose derivatives serve as complementary counter-materials, enabling transient TENG-based soft bioelectronic systems [64,67]. In addition, hydrogels, which are water-absorbent polymer networks with mechanical properties similar to biological tissues, provide a compliant, tissue-mimetic interface that is advantageous for soft implantable electronics [68]. Natural materials and other biopolymers have also been used as triboelectric layers because of their triboelectric and dielectric properties. The modification of polymers such as chitosan and cellulose could enhance their triboelectric properties, thereby aiding the design of a novel material with favorable properties [69]. Inorganic materials are primarily used to enhance electrical conduction and triboelectric performance. Metal foils such as Al, Au, and Cu commonly serve as electrodes to facilitate charge collection and transport, providing the stability required for implantable devices. While traditional Au electrodes offer excellent conductivity and stability, biodegradable Mg alloys are particularly attractive for transient implantable TENGs because they combine good electrical conductivity with in vivo degradability, allowing the device to dissolve after completing its therapeutic function [57]. Furthermore, inorganic nanostructures such as zinc oxide, copper oxide, and silver nanoparticles are often incorporated into flexible substrates to increase effective surface area and enhance triboelectric charge generation, thereby improving overall device performance [70,71]. Importantly, polymers such as PDMS, PTFE, and FEP, despite their favorable biocompatibility and chemical stability, remain non-resorbable in physiological conditions. As a result, they are incorporated into a biodegradable scaffold, such as lipids, proteins, and polysaccharides, to minimize the residual material burden. The biological fate of implantable bioelectronics should therefore be evaluated at the device level rather than the material level, considering the degradation, clearance, and long-term tissue response of all implanted components, including substrates, electrodes, conductors, encapsulation layers, adhesives, and interconnects [72,73].

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Self-powered bioelectronics for peripheral nerve regeneration: Electroactive materials, energy transduction, and therapeutic mechanisms》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Future perspectives and conclusions · p0275】Three decades of incremental progress in passive nerve conduits have yielded a frustrating ceiling: hollow tubes and collagen scaffolds reliably bridge short gaps but consistently fail to restore the electrophysiological fidelity that meaningful motor and sensory recovery demands. The past decade's pivot toward self-powered bioelectronic neuromodulation has fundamentally reframed this problem, shifting the design question from “how do we guide axons?” to “how do we recreate the endogenous bioelectric landscape that drives regeneration?” Galvanic cells, triboelectric nanogenerators, and piezoelectric nanogenerators each represent a distinct answer to that question, and their comparative strengths and limitations now define the frontier of the field.

【Future perspectives and conclusions · p0280】Of the three strategies, self-electrified galvanic devices offer a relatively simple strategy for movement-independent postoperative stimulation. They require no patient compliance, no external hardware, and no activity-dependent mechanical deformation. They simply activate upon contact with physiological fluids and deliver continuous DC stimulation while reactants and electrical continuity remain available. This simplicity is also their most significant constraint: output profile, stimulation duration, and degradation kinetics are largely fixed by material choice at the time of fabrication, leaving little room for post-implantation adjustment [119,120]. The transition from magnesium-to zinc-based anodes has meaningfully extended operational windows and reduced hydrogen evolution, and architectures that couple galvanic stimulation with integrated neural recording provide a basis for future responsive therapy, but recording alone does not establish a closed loop. Nevertheless, the field has yet to demonstrate reliable stimulation delivery calibrated to the weeks-long regeneration timeline in large-animal or human nerve injury contexts, and this remains the central translational bottleneck.
